html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Diagnose a stuck rollout with rollout status, history and undo
  • Spot probe, image, ConfigMap and Secret mistakes
  • Use port-forward, exec, previous logs and ephemeral containers
  • Separate an application fault from a platform fault, in Helm and GitOps too

2Stuck and failed rollouts, rollout status, history and undo, the progress deadline

Running case

A Harbor Books Release Sticks

  • A new storefront release stalls: the old Pods are still there, and some new Pods never become Ready
  • Customers still see the old version, and the team must choose: fix forward or roll back
  • The same release also goes through Helm and a GitOps agent, so the failure may show up in either tool
  • In this module you find out why, and who owns the fix

Stuck and Failed Rollouts

  • A rollout can stall because of quota, readiness probe failures, image pull errors, permissions, limit ranges or application misconfiguration
  • progressDeadlineSeconds is how long the controller waits before it reports no progress; it defaults to 600 seconds
  • Kubernetes only reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded; it does not roll back for you
  • rollout status watches, rollout history lists revisions, rollout undo goes back

Exam tip: Status to see it, history to choose, undo to go back.

3Probe misconfiguration

Probes That Misbehave

Probe When it is wrong
Liveness too strict: healthy containers are restarted, which can cause cascading failures under load
Readiness failing: the Pod is removed from the EndpointSlices, so Services send it no traffic, and a rollout cannot finish
Startup missing for a slow starter: the liveness probe may kill the container before it is up
  • Liveness does not wait for readiness: use initialDelaySeconds or a startup probe
  • A readiness probe that never succeeds shows up as new Pods that never become Ready

Exam tip: Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts.

4Image, ConfigMap and Secret errors

Image, ConfigMap and Secret Errors

Symptom Likely cause First move
ImagePullBackOff wrong image name or tag, or a private registry with no imagePullSecret fix the reference or add the secret
CrashLoopBackOff an application error, or a configuration error such as a wrong environment variable or a missing file logs --previous, then the settings
Event about a Secret the referenced Secret does not exist; the kubelet keeps retrying create it before the Pods that need it
Empty value an optional ConfigMap or key is missing create it, or check the key name

Exam tip: Read the Pod's events first: they name the missing image or Secret.

5Logs, exec, port-forward, kubectl debug and ephemeral containers

Looking Inside a Running Application

  • logs --previous shows the last output of the crashed container
  • exec opens a shell in a container, if the image has a shell
  • port-forward connects a local port to a port in a Pod, to test the application directly
  • kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container to a running Pod, which helps when the image has no shell

Four ways to look at an application

kubectl logs orders --previous
kubectl exec -it orders -- sh
kubectl port-forward pods/orders 8080:80
kubectl debug -it orders --image=busybox --target=orders

Exam tip: exec needs a shell in the image; debug brings its own.

6OOMKilled and CPU throttling

Resource Problems: OOMKilled and Throttling

  • Memory: over its limit, the container may be killed, with the reason OOMKilled, and then restarted
  • CPU: the limit is enforced by throttling: the container is slowed, not killed
  • A throttled container is slow, while an OOM-killed container restarts
  • Check kubectl top and the limits, then raise them or fix the application

Exam tip: Over the memory limit: killed. Over the CPU limit: slowed.

7Helm release failures, GitOps sync failures, application fault versus platform fault

Helm and GitOps Failures

  • Helm: with --wait, a release is marked FAILED if its Pods are not ready within the timeout, five minutes by default; helm history shows it and helm rollback returns
  • GitOps: OutOfSync means the cluster differs from Git; Degraded means resources are failing, for example a crash loop
  • The two are independent: an application can be Synced and Degraded, or OutOfSync after a webhook changed an object

Exam tip: OutOfSync is about Git; Degraded is about the workload.

Application Fault or Platform Fault?

  • Ask first: did the container start? If not, look at scheduling, image pull, volumes, quota, permissions and the node
  • If it started and then failed, look at the logs, configuration, probes and memory
  • Events point to the platform; logs point to the application
  • A failed Helm or GitOps release is usually one of these two, seen through a tool

Exam tip: Events for the platform, logs for the application.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1A rollout is stuck, and the progress deadline has passed. What does Kubernetes do?

  • AIt rolls the Deployment back to the previous revision on its own, and it deletes the new ReplicaSet with its Pods
  • BIt reports the stall in the status with the reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded, and takes no other action
  • CIt scales the Deployment to zero until someone fixes the Pod template of the release
  • DIt restarts every node that runs a Pod of the Deployment, so that the update can finish
Show the answer

Answer: B. After the deadline the Progressing condition becomes False with the reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Kubernetes does not roll back by itself, although a higher-level tool can act on the condition.

S2The new Harbor Books storefront release is stuck, and the team wants to return to the previous version quickly. Which command does that?

  • Akubectl rollout status deployment/storefront, which watches the progress of the rollout
  • Bkubectl rollout history deployment/storefront, which lists the revisions that exist
  • Ckubectl delete deployment storefront, which removes the Deployment and its Pods
  • Dkubectl rollout undo deployment/storefront, which goes back to the previous revision
Show the answer

Answer: D. The undo command returns the Deployment to its previous revision. Status and history only show information, and deleting the Deployment removes the application instead of restoring it.

S3New Pods of a Deployment keep failing their readiness probe, although their logs show no errors. What is the effect?

  • AThe Pods receive no Service traffic, because they are removed from the EndpointSlices, and the rollout cannot finish
  • BThe kubelet restarts the Pods again and again, because a readiness failure is treated as a crash
  • CThe Pods are evicted from their nodes at once, because the scheduler reads the probe results
  • DThe Deployment is scaled up automatically, because failing Pods count as extra demand
Show the answer

Answer: A. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the EndpointSlices of its Services, so it gets no traffic and does not count as ready for the rollout. Restarts come from failing liveness probes.

S4A Harbor Books Pod stays in an error state, and its events say that the Secret it references does not exist. What should the team do?

  • ARaise the memory limit of the container, because a missing Secret means that the container has too little memory
  • BAdd a readiness probe to the Pod, so that the kubelet can find the Secret by itself
  • CCreate the Secret in the namespace of the Pod, and the kubelet will retry running the Pod
  • DDelete the node that runs the Pod, so that its Secrets are copied to another node
Show the answer

Answer: C. The kubelet keeps retrying a Pod whose Secret cannot be fetched and reports an Event, so creating the Secret fixes it. Memory limits, probes and nodes are unrelated to a missing Secret.

S5The image of a Pod has no shell, so kubectl exec cannot open one. Which command lets the team troubleshoot inside that Pod?

  • Akubectl port-forward, which forwards a local port to a port in the Pod
  • Bkubectl debug, which adds an ephemeral container with its own tools to the Pod
  • Ckubectl rollout undo, which returns the Deployment to the previous revision and replaces the Pods again
  • Dkubectl top pod, which shows the CPU and memory use of the Pod
Show the answer

Answer: B. The debug command adds an ephemeral container with its own image and shell to a running Pod. Port forwarding tests connectivity, undo changes the revision, and top shows resource use.

S6A Harbor Books container is restarted again and again, and its last state shows the reason OOMKilled. What does that tell the team?

  • AThe node ran out of disk space, so the kubelet evicted the Pod from the node and started it again elsewhere
  • BThe image could not be pulled from the registry, so the container was never able to start at all
  • CThe container reached its CPU limit and was throttled until it stopped working and had to restart
  • DThe container used more memory than its limit, so the team should check for a leak or raise the limit
Show the answer

Answer: D. OOMKilled means that the container used more memory than its limit allowed. A CPU limit slows a container down but does not kill it, an image problem shows as ImagePullBackOff, and node-pressure eviction ends the Pod rather than restarting a container.

S7A GitOps tool shows an application as Synced but Degraded. What does that tell you?

  • AThe cluster matches what is in Git, but some resources are failing, for example a crash-looping Pod
  • BThe cluster differs from Git, and the tool has not yet been told to apply the change
  • CThe Git repository is unreachable, so the tool is unable to compare the cluster with it
  • DThe sync itself failed, so the tool left the resources of the application unchanged
Show the answer

Answer: A. Sync status asks whether the cluster matches Git, and health asks whether the resources work. Synced with Degraded means the manifests were applied but a workload, such as a crash-looping Pod, is unhealthy.
